title: The Gupta Empire
description: An illustrated map of the Gupta Empire, from Chandragupta I and the Licchavis through Samudragupta’s campaigns, Chandragupta II, Faxian, Kalidasa and Aryabhata, to the Huna invasions and the empire’s break-up in the 6th century CE.
mapLabel: Illustrated map of the Gupta Empire, from about 300 to about 550 CE
note: Based on inscriptions, coins and monuments, the accounts of Chinese pilgrims such as Faxian and Xuanzang, and later plays and legends; each chapter says which it follows. Reign dates are approximate, and the order of the later kings is debated. The map is stylised and not to scale; the areas under Powers are painted loosely and are not borders.

steps.title: A divided north
steps.text: About 300 CE, no single power held northern India. Later Kushan kings ruled the north-west, Naga kings ruled around Mathura and Padmavati, and Shaka Kshatrapas held Malwa and Gujarat. Gupta inscriptions name the family’s first rulers, Sri Gupta and Ghatotkacha, simply as great kings (maharaja). Where they ruled is debated: Magadha, eastern Uttar Pradesh and Bengal are all proposed.
steps.today: Today: Patna, Bihar, India, on the Ganga.

steps.title: A Licchavi queen
steps.text: Chandragupta I, Ghatotkacha’s son, married Kumaradevi, a princess of the Licchavis, an old ruling clan of Vaishali. Gold coins show the king and queen together, with the word Licchavayah (“the Licchavis”) on the back. Their son Samudragupta called himself “daughter’s son of the Licchavis” (Licchavi-dauhitra), so the marriage evidently brought prestige, and perhaps land.
steps.today: Today: Vaishali, north of Patna, Bihar.

steps.title: Great king of kings
steps.text: Chandragupta I was the first of his line to take the title great king of kings (maharajadhiraja). Gupta inscriptions count years in an era that begins in 319–320 CE, probably from his accession. The Puranas say the Guptas held the lands along the Ganga: Prayaga, Saketa and Magadha. Pataliputra seems to have been their capital.
steps.today: Today: Patna; Saketa is near Ayodhya, Uttar Pradesh.

steps.title: Chosen before the court
steps.text: Most of what we know of Samudragupta comes from a praise poem (prashasti) by his officer Harishena, carved on an Ashokan pillar now in the fort at Prayagraj. It says his father embraced him before the court and told him to rule the whole earth. Coins of a king Kacha may belong to a rival brother, or to Samudragupta himself.
steps.today: Today: the Allahabad pillar, in the fort at Prayagraj, Uttar Pradesh. It may first have stood at Kaushambi.

steps.title: Kings of the north uprooted
steps.text: Harishena says Samudragupta violently uprooted nine kings of the north (Aryavarta), and names them, among them Achyuta, Nagasena and Ganapatinaga. Coins of Naga kings such as Ganapatinaga are found at Padmavati and Mathura. Their lands seem to have been taken into the empire, which now ran along the Ganga plain from near Mathura to Bengal.
steps.today: Today: Pawaya, near Gwalior, Madhya Pradesh.

steps.title: The southern campaign
steps.text: The inscription lists twelve kings of the south (dakshinapatha), among them Mahendragiri of Pishtapura, Hastivarman of Vengi and Vishnugopa of Kanchi, a Pallava. Samudragupta, it says, captured them, then freed and restored them. He took tribute, not land. Historians debate the route, and whether he really reached Kanchi, far down the eastern coast.
steps.today: Today: Kanchipuram, Tamil Nadu; Pishtapura is Pithapuram, Andhra Pradesh.

steps.title: Tribute from the frontiers
steps.text: Frontier kings of Samatata, Davaka, Kamarupa, Nepala and Kartripura paid tribute, Harishena says, as did republics in the west such as the Malavas and Yaudheyas. Further off, the Kushan ruler, the Shakas and the people of Sri Lanka sent gifts and sought charters bearing the Gupta seal of Garuda. How far this was real power, not courtly boasting, is debated.
steps.today: Today: Kamarupa is around Guwahati, Assam; Samatata is in south-eastern Bangladesh.

steps.title: A monastery for Lanka’s pilgrims
steps.text: A Chinese account says Meghavarna, king of Sri Lanka, sent gifts to Samudragupta and asked leave to build a monastery at Bodh Gaya, where the Buddha found enlightenment, for pilgrims from his island. It was granted. Xuanzang, visiting about 637, describes a great monastery there built by a king of Sri Lanka, home to about a thousand monks.
steps.today: Today: Bodh Gaya, Bihar; the Mahabodhi temple is a World Heritage Site.

steps.title: The horse and the lyre
steps.text: Samudragupta’s gold coins show a horse before a sacrificial post, marking a horse sacrifice (ashvamedha), which later Gupta inscriptions say he revived after long neglect. Another coin shows him seated, playing a lyre (vina). Harishena calls him king of poets (kaviraja), skilled in music. Gupta gold coins, based on the Kushan weight, are among the finest of ancient India.
steps.today: Today: Gupta gold coins are in museums in India, London and elsewhere.

steps.title: Ramagupta and Dhruvadevi
steps.text: A play, the Devichandraguptam, survives only in quotations. In it, King Ramagupta, Samudragupta’s elder son, agrees to hand his queen Dhruvadevi to a Shaka king. His brother Chandragupta goes in her place, disguised, and kills the Shaka, later killing Ramagupta and marrying Dhruvadevi. Copper coins and Jain images near Vidisha do name a great king Ramagupta.
steps.today: Today: Vidisha, Madhya Pradesh; the images were found at Durjanpur nearby.

steps.title: The end of the Shaka Kshatrapas
steps.text: Chandragupta II, who took the title Vikramaditya (“sun of valour”), conquered the Western Kshatrapas, ending three centuries of Shaka rule in Malwa and Gujarat. The last Kshatrapa coins are those of Rudrasimha III. In the west Chandragupta issued silver coins in the Kshatrapa style, with Garuda in place of their emblem. Ujjain became a great Gupta city.
steps.today: Today: Ujjain, Madhya Pradesh.

steps.title: The boar at Udayagiri
steps.text: In caves cut into a hill near Vidisha, a giant relief shows Vishnu as a boar (Varaha) lifting the earth goddess from the waters. One cave inscription, dated 401 CE, records a gift by a local chief who served Chandragupta II. Another says the minister Virasena came here with the king, who wished to conquer the whole world.
steps.today: Today: the Udayagiri caves, near Vidisha, Madhya Pradesh.

steps.title: A daughter in the Deccan
steps.text: Chandragupta II married his daughter Prabhavatigupta to Rudrasena II, king of the Vakatakas of the Deccan. When Rudrasena died young, she ruled for their sons as regent for over a decade. Her copper-plate charters name her father’s Gupta line before her husband’s. The alliance kept the Guptas’ southern flank safe while they fought in the west.
steps.today: Today: Nagardhan, near Ramtek, Nagpur district, Maharashtra.

steps.title: Faxian in the Middle Kingdom
steps.text: The Chinese monk Faxian came to India for Buddhist texts. In the middle country, he wrote, people were prosperous, punishments were mostly fines, and few killed animals; Chandalas lived apart. At Pataliputra he saw Ashoka’s palace and free hospitals funded by leading families. He never names the king, presumably Chandragupta II. He sailed home by Sri Lanka.
steps.today: Today: Patna, Bihar. Faxian’s account is the Foguoji, “Record of Buddhist Kingdoms”.

steps.title: The iron pillar
steps.text: An iron pillar over seven metres tall stands in Delhi, made with such skill that it has hardly rusted in sixteen centuries. Its inscription praises a king Chandra, usually taken to be Chandragupta II, who fought the Vangas in the east and crossed the seven mouths of the Indus. It was probably moved to Delhi from elsewhere centuries later.
steps.today: Today: in the Qutb Minar complex, Mehrauli, Delhi.

steps.title: Kalidasa
steps.text: Kalidasa, the greatest poet and playwright in Sanskrit, wrote Shakuntala and The Cloud Messenger (Meghaduta), in which an exiled yaksha sends a cloud from Ramagiri to the Himalaya, asking it to turn aside for Ujjain. His dates are debated, but most scholars place him in the Gupta age. Late tradition sets him among Vikramaditya’s nine gems.
steps.today: Today: Ujjain holds an annual Kalidasa festival; Ramagiri is usually placed at Ramtek.

steps.title: Kumaragupta and Nalanda
steps.text: Kumaragupta I ruled for about forty years, mostly in peace, and issued more kinds of gold coin than any Gupta, some showing him feeding a peacock. Xuanzang says Nalanda was founded by a king Shakraditya, whom many historians identify with Kumaragupta. It grew into the greatest Buddhist university in Asia, and seals of later Gupta kings were found there.
steps.today: Today: Nalanda Mahavihara, Bihar, a World Heritage Site.

steps.title: The silk weavers’ temple
steps.text: A guild of silk weavers moved from Lata, on the Gujarat coast, to Dashapura. In 436, under Kumaragupta and his governor Bandhuvarman, they built a temple to the sun, and their poet Vatsabhatti wrote its inscription. Some, it says, became archers, storytellers or astrologers. In 473 the guild repaired the temple. It is a rare look at ordinary townspeople.
steps.today: Today: Mandsaur, Madhya Pradesh.

steps.title: Skandagupta and the Hunas
steps.text: Skandagupta’s pillar at Bhitari says that when he restored his family’s shaken fortunes he spent a night on the bare earth, and that when he met the Hunas, Central Asian invaders, in close combat the earth shook. He went to his weeping mother, it says, as Krishna to Devaki. Whether his succession was disputed is debated.
steps.today: Today: Bhitari, Ghazipur district, Uttar Pradesh.

steps.title: Repairing Sudarshana lake
steps.text: In 455, heavy rain burst the dam of Sudarshana lake below Girnar. Chakrapalita, son of Skandagupta’s governor Parnadatta, rebuilt it within a year and raised a temple to Vishnu. The record was carved on the rock that already bore Ashoka’s edicts and Rudradaman’s account of his own repair: three empires mending one lake over seven centuries.
steps.today: Today: the Ashoka edict rock, Junagadh, Gujarat; the lake is lost.

steps.title: The Buddhas of Sarnath
steps.text: At Sarnath, where the Buddha first taught, workshops carved the calm, graceful Buddha that became a model across Asia. Two standing Buddhas given by the monk Abhayamitra are dated to the reigns of Kumaragupta II and Budhagupta, in 474 and 477. The seated Buddha turning the wheel of the teaching, from the same century, is Sarnath’s most famous.
steps.today: Today: the Sarnath Museum, near Varanasi, Uttar Pradesh.

steps.title: Buying land in Bengal
steps.text: Copper plates found at Damodarpur record land bought from the government, dated from Kumaragupta I into the 6th century. Each sale passed through a district office whose council included the chief merchant, the caravan leader, the chief artisan and the chief scribe (kayastha). They show the empire run through governors and local councils, with townspeople sharing the work.
steps.today: Today: Damodarpur, Dinajpur district, Bangladesh.

steps.title: Eran changes sides
steps.text: In 484, under Budhagupta, the brothers Matrivishnu and Dhanyavishnu raised a pillar to Vishnu at Eran, crowned with Garuda. A few years later Dhanyavishnu carved another inscription, on a huge stone boar, dated to the first year of Toramana, king of the Hunas. The same family now served a new overlord: central India had slipped from the Guptas.
steps.today: Today: Eran, Sagar district, Madhya Pradesh.

steps.title: Aryabhata at Kusumapura
steps.text: Aryabhata wrote that he was 23 when he finished his Aryabhatiya, in 499. Working at Kusumapura, usually taken as Pataliputra, he gave pi as 3.1416, said the earth turns on its axis, and explained eclipses by the shadows of the earth and moon. His verses use place value, and they shaped Indian astronomy for centuries.
steps.today: Today: Patna; India’s first satellite, launched in 1975, was named Aryabhata.

steps.title: A temple of stone
steps.text: Gupta-age builders turned from caves and wood to free-standing stone temples. The Dashavatara temple at Deogarh, one of the earliest, once had a tower over its shrine. Its panels show Vishnu asleep on the serpent Ananta, Vishnu rescuing the elephant king, and the sages Nara and Narayana. Its date is debated; most put it near 500.
steps.today: Today: Deogarh, Lalitpur district, Uttar Pradesh.

steps.title: Goparaja’s memorial
steps.text: A stone at Eran, dated 510, says Goparaja followed a king Bhanugupta into a great battle and was killed, and that his wife followed him into the fire. It is the oldest dated record of a widow’s death on her husband’s pyre (sati). Who Bhanugupta was, and whom he fought, possibly the Hunas, is not certain.
steps.today: Today: Eran, Sagar district, Madhya Pradesh.

steps.title: Mihirakula
steps.text: Toramana’s son Mihirakula ruled the Hunas in India from Shakala. Xuanzang, a century later, remembered him as a cruel persecutor of Buddhists. He says Mihirakula marched on Magadha, whose king Baladitya, often identified with Narasimhagupta, captured him and let him go. Mihirakula then seized Kashmir. An inscription at Gwalior is dated in his reign.
steps.today: Today: Sialkot, Punjab, Pakistan.

steps.title: Yashodharman’s pillars
steps.text: Yashodharman, a king of Dashapura, raised two victory pillars at nearby Sondani. They claim he ruled lands that neither the Guptas nor the Hunas had held, from the Himalaya to the sea, and that Mihirakula bowed at his feet. His power did not last long, but the boast itself shows how far the Guptas had fallen.
steps.today: Today: the Sondani pillars, near Mandsaur, Madhya Pradesh.

steps.title: The last Guptas
steps.text: Vishnugupta, about 550, is the last known Gupta king. Successors divided the empire: the Maukharis at Kannauj, the Maitrakas at Valabhi, founded by a Gupta general, and the so-called Later Guptas in Magadha, whose link to the old line is unknown. When Xuanzang came about 637, he found Pataliputra largely in ruins.
steps.today: Today: Patna, Bihar, the capital of the state.

steps.title: A golden age?
steps.text: The Puranas barely remembered the Guptas. In the 1830s scholars in Calcutta, among them James Prinsep, read the Allahabad pillar and other Gupta inscriptions, and the empire returned to history. Later historians called it India’s golden age. Many now prefer classical age: the art and learning were real, but so were land grants to Brahmins and harder caste rules.
steps.today: Today: the Allahabad pillar still stands in the fort at Prayagraj.

items.name: Chandragupta I
items.life: Ruled from about 319 CE, probably to about 335
items.text: Son of Ghatotkacha, Chandragupta I was the first Gupta to call himself great king of kings. His marriage to the Licchavi princess Kumaradevi was celebrated on gold coins, and the Gupta era probably counts from his accession. He chose his son Samudragupta as heir, Harishena says, before the assembled court.

items.name: Kumaradevi
items.text: A princess of the Licchavis, Kumaradevi married Chandragupta I. She is one of the few queens of ancient India shown on coins beside her husband. Her son Samudragupta named his mother’s family in his titles, which suggests the Licchavis brought the young dynasty real standing.

items.name: Samudragupta
items.text: Samudragupta made the Guptas an empire. Harishena’s poem lists the northern kings he uprooted, the southern kings he captured and freed, and the frontier rulers who paid him tribute. His coins show him as archer, tiger-slayer and lyre player. Some modern writers have called him India’s Napoleon, a comparison many historians find unhelpful.

items.name: Harishena
items.text: Harishena held high office under Samudragupta, including minister for peace and war, and composed the praise poem on the Prayagraj pillar, part verse and part prose. It is our main source for the reign, and like all such poems it was written to glorify the king.

items.name: Meghavarna
items.text: Meghavarna, called Sirimeghavanna in the Sri Lankan chronicles, ruled at Anuradhapura. The chronicles say the Buddha’s tooth relic reached the island in his reign. A Chinese source says he sent an embassy to Samudragupta for leave to build a monastery for Sri Lankan pilgrims at Bodh Gaya.

items.name: Chandragupta II
items.text: Chandragupta II took the west from the Shaka Kshatrapas and bound the Vakatakas to him by marriage. His reign is often seen as the Gupta peak, the time Faxian visited and, many think, of Kalidasa. Later legends of a king Vikramaditya of Ujjain may partly remember him, though they mix in other kings.

items.name: Dhruvadevi
items.text: Dhruvadevi was Chandragupta II’s queen and the mother of Kumaragupta I, as Gupta seals record. The play Devichandraguptam makes her first the wife of Ramagupta, rescued from a Shaka king by Chandragupta. Whether that story is history or drama is still argued.

items.name: Prabhavatigupta
items.text: Daughter of Chandragupta II and the Naga princess Kuberanaga, Prabhavatigupta married the Vakataka king Rudrasena II. Widowed young, she ruled for her sons and issued land grants in her own name, proudly giving her Gupta descent. She lived to see her son Pravarasena II on the throne.

items.name: Faxian
items.text: Faxian set out from China about 399, already in his sixties, to find complete rules for monks. He crossed Central Asia, spent years in India copying texts, and returned by sea through Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia. His short account is the oldest surviving eyewitness description of Gupta India.

items.name: Kalidasa
items.text: Kalidasa wrote the play Shakuntala, the long poems Raghuvamsha and Kumarasambhava, and The Cloud Messenger. Almost nothing about his life is certain; later legends make him a fool turned genius by the goddess Kali. His Shakuntala, translated into English in 1789, made Sanskrit literature famous in Europe.

items.name: Kumaragupta I
items.text: Son of Chandragupta II and Dhruvadevi, Kumaragupta I held the empire together for about forty years. He took the title Mahendraditya and performed a horse sacrifice. Many identify him with the Shakraditya who, Xuanzang says, founded Nalanda. The Hunas seem to have threatened only towards the end of his reign.

items.name: Skandagupta
items.text: Skandagupta is remembered as the king who threw back the Hunas. His inscriptions at Bhitari and Junagadh tell of restoring the family’s fortunes and repairing the great lake below Girnar. His gold coins are lighter in gold than earlier ones, perhaps a sign of the strain of war.

items.name: Aryabhata
items.text: Aryabhata wrote the Aryabhatiya, 121 short verses on arithmetic, algebra, trigonometry and astronomy. He held that the earth spins and that eclipses are shadows, not demons, ideas later astronomers often rejected. His tables of sines and his methods spread to the Islamic world and, from there, influenced Europe.

items.name: Mihirakula
items.role: King of the Hunas in India
items.text: Son of Toramana, Mihirakula ruled from Shakala. The Greek traveller Cosmas Indicopleustes heard of a Huna king in India with two thousand elephants. Xuanzang and the Kashmiri chronicle Rajatarangini paint him as cruel. Defeated by Yashodharman and, it seems, by a Gupta king, he ended his days in Kashmir.

items.name: Yashodharman
items.text: Yashodharman of the Aulikara family is known almost only from his inscriptions at Mandsaur and Sondani, dated around 532. They claim an empire wider than the Guptas’ and the humbling of Mihirakula. No later record speaks of his successors, and his power seems to have ended with him.
